newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - Iraq seen weighing on market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - Iraq seen weighing on market.

text.p: U.S. crude prices are expected to weaken this week now that the United Nations has completed the key element in renewing the "oil-for-food" deal with Iraq.
Benchmark U.S. West Texas Intermediate/Cushing fell below $19.00 early Monday,s down more than 30 cents, on news that the U.N. and Iraq reached agreement on aid distribution.

Market expectations see Iraqi oil sales restarting within two weeks of Annan's approval, putting Baghdad's oil on the market by early August, though not delivered to the U.S. market until September at the earliest.
"Everything is now in the market (once Iraq oil returns), with Iraq and the OPEC meeting," said Tom Bentz, head of energy trading for High Yield Analytics in New York.
Cash dealers forecast sour barrels in the U.S. Gulf would slip when Baghdad resumed liftings, causing a weakening ripple from the Mediterranean.

"I'm surprised West Texas Sour/Midland hasn't taken more of a hit, but I guess people are waiting for the actual oil to hit the market. There is still some unease over the timing, of course, and whether things will go that smoothly," said a cash dealer in the U.S. Gulf.
The U.N. official in Baghdad said Monday that he expected the aid plan to be delivered to the U.N. secretary-general, Kofi Annan, by next Monday.

Annan must then approve it, followed by approval of a new oil price formula and individual oil sales contracts. The whole process could take a matter of a few days and oil sales could resume by the end of next week, but that is the optimistic view, market analysts said.

The benchmark U.S. sour, West Texas Sour/Midland, traded at a barely-changed differential of $1.32 and $1.31 below WTI/Cushing early Monday. Dealers said the force majeure on Colombian Cano Limon barrels following pipeline damage due to rebel attackes, is partly offsetting the Iraq effect, at least in the short term.

Meanwhile, Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James continued to find support at around a 20 cents premium to the August benchmark. As the price for LLS maintains its strength, U.S. refiners seem to be showing more interest in alternative North Sea Brent and Colombian Cusiana crude.
Statoil on Friday sold the last of five Brent cargoes off a ULCC arriving July 15-20 with a Gulf Coast refiner, traders said.
The cargo was heard sold at August West Texas Intermediate/Cushing minus 25-30 cents a barrel.
On Thursday, the same company sold two half cargoes of 250,000 barrels each of Norwegian Oseberg to two Gulf Coast refiners at 40-50 cents under WTI/Cushing for end-July delivery, traders said.
Meanwhile, equity producer Total last Thursday sold a Cusiana cargo to a U.S. refiner at October WTI minus 85-90 cents a barrel fob, traders said. The 550,000 cargo loads August 16-20.
